title: Subject attribution, tense and modality — the acceptance target for a future engine session
what_this_measures: Whether the engine can tell a statement ABOUT THIS PRODUCT, NOW, from a statement about a sibling product, the packaging, the shipment, a bundled item, a competitor, the industry, a reviewer, the whole range, or about this product at a different time or in a different mood. It is stated as EXPECTED outcomes, not measured ones: this suite is a target, not a description of today's engine.
what_this_does_not_measure: VALUE. Not one of these sentences has been measured against real merchant copy. See `frequency_caveat` — it is the most important field in this file and it is deliberately not in a footnote.

frequency_caveat.statement: THIS SUITE MEASURES CAPABILITY, NOT VALUE. A fix that passes every case here has been shown to be POSSIBLE, not shown to be WORTH SHIPPING. Before shipping, a natural-frequency read against real merchant copy is required, in both directions: how often does each hostile shape actually occur, and how many TRUE statements does the fix cost?
frequency_caveat.precedent: The `origin` tombstone. A narrowing that closed every false pass in hand-built sets was measured against 5,322 real product descriptions and found to cost 17 true statements for 0 false passes gained; the class it closed had ZERO instances across all 5,322 products. The term was removed. A hand-built set could not have arbitrated that, and this is a hand-built set.
frequency_caveat.second_precedent: v2.6 built a full negation-scope rewrite and measured 16/16 denials and 12/12 truths on ITS OWN set. An independent pass then measured it as a NET REGRESSION: 7 false passes v2.5 caught and it did not, plus 46 false fails. Passing your own suite is evidence about the suite.
frequency_caveat.consequence: A green run here is a licence to MEASURE, never a licence to ship.

terms.note: PINNED DELIBERATELY. Subject and tense handling is a property of the ENGINE, not of any vocabulary, so this suite carries its own term list rather than loading one. If it loaded `decaf-method.json` then a future narrowing of that vocabulary would silently change what this suite measures, and a fix could appear to pass because a term moved. Seven terms, chosen to cover all four term shapes the attack templatizer distinguishes.
terms.drift_tripwire: `acceptance.test.ts` asserts every pinned term is still a supporting term in the source vocabulary. If that assertion fails, the vocabulary was narrowed and this suite must be RE-DERIVED — it is not a licence to edit the assertion.

strata.sibling_product: the property is stated of ANOTHER product the seller stocks
strata.packaging: the property is stated of the packaging
strata.shipment: the property is stated of the delivery, not the thing delivered
strata.bundled_item: the property is stated of one item inside a multi-item listing
strata.competitor: the property is stated of a named other company
strata.industry_generic: the property is stated of the category at large, usually as a warning
strata.review_quote: the property is stated by a buyer, not by the seller
strata.site_wide: the property is stated of the whole range, not this unit
strata.subscription: the property appears in purchase-widget copy
strata.cross_sell: the property is stated of a product being cross-sold
strata.comparative: the property is stated of a comparison class this product is measured against
strata.past_tense: the property held in the past and the sentence says so
strata.future_conditional: the property is an intention or a conditional offer
strata.modal: the property is a possibility or an option on request
strata.enquiry_evaluation: the seller asked about or is trialling the property
strata.plain_present: MUST NOT REGRESS — the ordinary present-tense claim
strata.spec_block: MUST NOT REGRESS — the specification-row form
strata.first_person: MUST NOT REGRESS — the seller's own voice
strata.trade_form: MUST NOT REGRESS — the listing conventions the trade actually uses
strata.temporal_but_current: MUST NOT REGRESS — a present claim carrying temporal words. The shape a tense fix is most likely to break
strata.already_refused: MUST NOT REGRESS — hostile shapes the engine refuses TODAY. A fix that closes the new classes while unwiring these is the v2.6 result exactly

cases.text: Our Ethiopian decaf uses the Swiss Water Process.
cases.why: One line of ordinary copy about a different coffee, on a page for this one. The subject is `Our Ethiopian decaf`, and it is not this product.

cases.text: Our house decaf is a Swiss Water Decaf; this Kenya is full caffeine.
cases.why: A sibling named and this product EXPLICITLY excluded. The semicolon is a clause boundary, so the exclusion is never read.

cases.text: Our Colombian lot is a Mountain Water Decaf.
cases.why: A named sibling with no contrastive marker at all — the hardest form, because nothing in the sentence signals that another product is meant.

cases.text: Our other decaf uses the Royal Select Water Process.
cases.why: `other` is the only word distinguishing this from a true claim, and it is not the matched term.

cases.text: Our packaging is made from Swiss Water Process kraft board.
cases.why: The subject is the packaging. Nonsense on its face, which is what makes it a fair test of whether the guard reads the subject rather than the keyword.

cases.text: Our Swiss Water Process decaf pouch is lined with recycled foil.
cases.why: The packaging class in the word order a merchant ACTUALLY writes, rather than the contrived form an adjacency test happens to catch.

cases.text: Every Mountain Water Decaf carton is printed with soy ink.
cases.why: The same with the container noun after the term rather than before it.

cases.text: Your shipment of Swiss Water Process decaf leaves the roastery within 24 hours.
cases.why: A sentence about getting the thing to the buyer is not a statement about the thing.

cases.text: Orders of our Mountain Water Decaf are dispatched the same day.
cases.why: The subject is the order. Logistics copy is on essentially every product page.

cases.text: The holiday hamper contains a Swiss Water Process decaf and two mugs.
cases.why: The property is named for one item inside a hamper and the row credits it to the hamper.

cases.text: The gift set that goes with this bag contains a Swiss Water Decaf.
cases.why: `goes with` is outside the related-product veto's closed phrase list.

cases.text: This starter kit includes a Mountain Water Decaf and a grinder.
cases.why: `kit includes` IS in the related-product veto, so this shape is expected to be refused today. Kept in the hostile set on purpose: a stratum with no already-closed member cannot show a fix UNWIRING one.

cases.text: Northbank Coffee uses the Swiss Water Process for their decaf; we do things differently.
cases.why: Competitor attribution credits another company's process to this product. The name is fictional deliberately — a committed test file should not manufacture claims about a real business.

cases.text: Northbank Coffee's decaf is decaffeinated with methylene chloride.
cases.why: The same class rewritten INTO the shipped frame. The decaf review's refuter measured this rewrite passing 13 of 13, which is what turned a class recorded as closed into a class recorded as open.

cases.text: Most supermarket coffee is decaffeinated with methylene chloride.
cases.why: A roaster disparaging the industry, recorded as disclosing its own method. The most reputationally damaging false pass available in this category.

cases.text: The cheapest decafs on the market are decaffeinated with methylene chloride.
cases.why: The same with a superlative subject rather than a quantifier.

cases.text: "The best Swiss Water Process decaf I have ever tried." — Sarah M.
cases.why: An attributed pull-quote carrying none of the review vocabulary the keyword veto is keyed on.

cases.text: "We switched to their Mountain Water Decaf and never looked back." — J. Okafor
cases.why: The same, and the buyer's voice is signalled only by the quotation marks and the attribution dash.

cases.text: All of our decafs use the Swiss Water Process.
cases.why: Roasters stock more than one decaf origin processed at more than one facility, so a statement about the range does not establish a fact about this lot.

cases.text: Every decaf we stock is a Mountain Water Decaf.
cases.why: The universal quantifier form. Arguably the weakest hostile case in the suite, since it entails the claim if true — which is exactly why an adjudicator should see it and decide.

cases.text: Choose a monthly subscription of our Swiss Water Process decaf.
cases.why: Purchase-widget copy avoiding every cadence phrase the subscription veto is keyed on.

cases.text: Our subscribers get the Mountain Water Decaf in month three.
cases.why: A rotation schedule, which says this product is what arrives in a DIFFERENT month.

cases.text: We also stock a Swiss Water Process decaf from Colombia.
cases.why: `also stock` is outside the related-product veto's closed phrase list, which covers `also available` and `also try`.

cases.text: We keep a Mountain Water Decaf on the shelf too.
cases.why: A cross-sell with no cross-sell verb at all.

cases.text: Sweeter than a typical Sugarcane EA lot.
cases.why: A comparison to a class is not a claim of membership in it. The comparative veto catches `unlike` and not `sweeter than`.

cases.text: Cleaner in the cup than most Swiss Water Process decafs.
cases.why: The same shape with the comparison class in the plural.

cases.text: Until 2024 we used the Swiss Water Process for this lot.
cases.why: Past tense says the process is no longer in use, and the row would report it as the method for what is on sale today.

cases.text: This coffee was a Mountain Water Decaf before we changed suppliers.
cases.why: A past copula plus an explicit change event. Nothing in the engine reads either.

cases.text: We used the Royal Select Water Process on last year's harvest.
cases.why: Past tense scoped to a different harvest — the subject and the tense both point away from this lot.

cases.text: We hope to move this coffee to the Swiss Water Process next season.
cases.why: An explicit future intention says the coffee is NOT currently processed this way.

cases.text: If you prefer a Swiss Water Process decaf, our sourcing team can find one.
cases.why: The plain meaning is that this coffee is not processed that way; the sentence offers to find one that is.

cases.text: We are switching to the Mountain Water Process later this year.
cases.why: A transition in progress says the CURRENT state is the other one.

cases.text: We may use the Swiss Water Process for future lots.
cases.why: A modal states a possibility, not a fact.

cases.text: This lot could be a Mountain Water Decaf next season.
cases.why: A conditional possibility scoped to a future season.

cases.text: Swiss Water Process decaf is available on request.
cases.why: Availability on request says the DEFAULT product is not this.

cases.text: We asked our importer about the Royal Select Water Process.
cases.why: The sentence records that a question was asked. It states nothing about how this coffee was decaffeinated.

cases.text: We are evaluating the Mountain Water Process for a future release.
cases.why: Evaluating a process is not using it, and the sentence says so plainly.

cases.text: Decaffeinated with the Swiss Water Process at a dedicated facility.
cases.why: The canonical true positive. If this stops passing, the fix has broken the ordinary case and is a net regression whatever it closed.

cases.text: This lot went through the Swiss Water Process before roasting.
cases.why: A past-tense VERB describing a completed step in making THIS product. The single most dangerous case in the suite for a naive tense rule: `went` is past, and the claim is current.

cases.text: Our Swiss Water Decaf comes from a single farm in Huila.
cases.why: A first-person possessive that is NOT a sibling reference — `Our X` is the commonest honest phrasing and the commonest sibling phrasing, and only the wider page distinguishes them.

cases.text: This lot is decaffeinated with methylene chloride, as disclosed by our importer.
cases.why: The honest disclosure of the unflattering answer. A fix that suppresses this suppresses exactly the transparency the standard exists to reward.

cases.text: Process: Swiss Water Process.
cases.why: The spec-row form. It has no finite verb and no subject at all, so any rule that requires a readable subject must fail OPEN here or it guts every specification-heavy category.

cases.text: Method: Mountain Water Process.
cases.why: The same shape under a different label, because a subject rule keyed on a specific spec-row word would pass `Process:` and fail `Method:` while looking like it had generalised.

cases.text: Decaffeination: Royal Select Water Process.
cases.why: The same where the label is the claim topic itself.

cases.text: We use the Swiss Water Process for every lot we sell.
cases.why: The seller's own voice with a universal quantifier — nearly identical in form to `sit-01`, which must NOT pass. If a fix cannot separate these two it has not solved the problem, it has moved it.

cases.text: We decaffeinate this coffee with the Mountain Water Process.
cases.why: First person with an explicit `this coffee` object.

cases.text: Every bag we sell is a Swiss Water Decaf.
cases.why: A universal over the seller's own units. The honest twin of `sit-02`.

cases.text: A Swiss Water Process decaf from Huila, roasted last week.
cases.why: The verbless listing form the specialty trade actually writes.

cases.text: Colombia Sugarcane EA decaf, washed at the mill.
cases.why: An origin-first listing line with no verb and no subject.

cases.text: Decaffeinated by the Mountain Water Process in Veracruz.
cases.why: A passive with the agent named and no surface subject.

cases.text: This decaf still uses the Swiss Water Process, as it always has.
cases.why: Carries `still` and `always has` — temporal vocabulary in a sentence whose claim is emphatically CURRENT. The shape a keyword-based tense rule breaks first.

cases.text: We have used the Swiss Water Process since 2019.
cases.why: Present perfect with a date. A rule keyed on `used` plus a year would refuse this and refuse `pst-01` and be unable to tell them apart.

cases.text: We do not offer a Swiss Water Process decaf in this range.
cases.why: The negation guard closes this TODAY. A fix that rewrites clause scope and unwires it has traded a new class for an old one — which is the v2.6 result exactly.

cases.text: One verified buyer said the Swiss Water Process version is the best decaf they have had.
cases.why: The review veto closes this today, keyed on `verified buyer`.

cases.text: We no longer offer a Swiss Water Process decaf.
cases.why: `no longer` is in the negator list, so the ONE tense-adjacent shape the engine already closes. A tense fix must keep it closed.

cases.text: Is the Swiss Water Process used for this coffee?
cases.why: An interrogative. `findSupport` drops questions, so this is closed today; it is here because an FAQ rewrite is a plausible side effect of a subject rule.
